Before God created time and space, there was no time at all. God's life, therefore, is not quantitative but qualitative. He does not exist for an infinite number of days along some endless timeline, because time itself did not exist prior to creation.

God cannot die not because He has accumulated unlimited time, but because He is immortal by nature—unaffected by sin or death, perfect, self-sufficient, and unchanging in who He is. His immortality flows from His very being, not from the length of His existence.

Likewise, in the resurrection, we will receive a new body that is immortal and life that is imperishable. We will no longer be vulnerable to sickness, aging, or death. We will become like God in the sense that nothing can destroy us:
When the perishable has been clothed with the imperishable... then the saying that is written will come true: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”
(1 Corinthians 15:54)

Eternal life, then, is not about living endless days. That is only a byproduct—a side effect. In its truest sense, eternal life is about sharing in a kind of life like God's own: a life that is untouchable by death, incorruptible by sin, and ultimately indestructible.
Conclusion: Think Like a Hebrew, Not a Greek

In conclusion, Augustine’s Neoplatonically shaped interpretation of olam and aion introduced a rigid, endless view of divine punishment into Western Christianity that departed sharply from the restorative justice envisioned in Jewish thought and preserved in some Eastern/Orthodox traditions. By equating God's infinite nature with infinite retribution, Augustine committed logical and linguistic errors that gave rise to the Western doctrine of eternal conscious torment. Yet the biblical and Jewish tradition reminds us that eternity is not about endless duration but about the quality of incorruptible life in God—a life that conquers death, restores creation, and embodies the victory of resurrection rather than the permanence of punishment.

To understand eternal life is to stop thinking like a Greek philosopher or a modern engineer and start thinking more like a Hebrew prophet and a Jewish rabbi. The Bible's vision of life is not primarily concerned with endless time but with blessedness, wholeness, closeness to God, and victory over death—immortality.
For us now—His disciples—eternal life is knowing God. It is living abundantly now (and forever) because nothing—not even death—can separate us from His love.
This is eternal life: life that reflects God's glory, shares His joy, and dwells in His presence with an immortal body.

chapters.title: Eternal Conscious Torment Fails the Test of God's Character

blocks.s: f an alien spent five minutes on social media today, he wouldn't be surprised to I discover that there are roughly 49,000 Christian groups and sects worldwide, since they rarely agree on much—especially on doctrines of salvation. But if one’s afterlife fate hinges on solving a theological puzzle that Christians themselves can hardly agree on, then salvation begins to resemble not a gift of grace but a cruel game of cosmic Russian roulette.
Such a vision portrays God not as a loving Father, but as the architect of something disturbingly close to an abusive experiment.
I will now present three theological arguments against the doctrine of Eternal Conscious Torment.
Eternal Conscious Torment Fails the Test of Divine Guardianship

God is our guardian because He created us, knows us, and sustains our every breath. We are under His responsibility. Like a faithful shepherd, He watches over what is His own—not from obligation, but from love. We are not self-made or forgotten; we are held, protected, and guided by the One who gave us Life.
Christians often use the analogy of God as a loving father. But let’s put this to the test.

A good parent teaches, nurtures, and corrects their child. Even if a child rebels, a loving parent does not abuse them by burning them in the fire or casting them into a torture chamber to suffer forever. If God is truly a better father than any human (Matthew 7:11), why would He operate by standards we would find abusive in any human relationship?

If we, as imperfect human beings, would never burn our own children alive for disobedience (unless we are psychopaths), how can we believe that a God of infinite love and mercy would commit something infinitely worse?

Even earthly parents know that when children misbehave, correction should be temporary and purposeful—aimed at growth. But punishment designed only to inflict endless suffering? That is not justice. That is cruelty. If hell truly meant infinite torment with no chance of healing or change, then it would serve no purpose except to gratify divine sadism. Yet Scripture teaches that God's justice is restorative, not vengeful; His love corrects, heals, forgives enemies, and seeks reconciliation. Unending torture accomplishes none of this.

This is the great divide between religion’s gospel of fear and the true Gospel of a God who is, in every way, mighty to save. If the primary purpose of human life is simply to avoid eternal conscious torment, then something is profoundly wrong with how we have imagined both God and ourselves. Life becomes a fearful escape room contest, not a meaningful journey; faith becomes anxiety, not transformation.

For what kind of loving God would torment most of humanity forever with no redemptive goal? Why would the One who commands us to forgive without limit (Matthew 5:44; Luke 17:4) refuse to forgive His own offspring and image? And how could infinite punishment be fair for finite beings—fragile minds shaped by trauma, culture, fear, misinformation, and distortion?

If God is a loving Father, then His justice must look like love. And if He created us with limited understanding, why assume that once we stand before Him—seeing clearly for the first time—we would not see, understand, repent, and turn to Him freely?
A theology built on fear collapses under its own contradictions. A theology built on love, restoration, and the character of Christ is the only one that makes sense of Scripture—and the human heart.
Eternal Conscious Torment Fails the Test of Redemptive Grace
We love to sing songs about the sweetness of God's amazing grace, but do we truly understand what grace means?

Human revenge is driven by emotion, which is why many find a dark comfort— and even a perverse satisfaction—in the idea of a monstrous god who tortures their enemies forever. The doctrine of Eternal Conscious Torment doesn’t reflect divine grace—it mirrors human vindictiveness. It satisfies something dark in us: the desire not just for justice, but for payback. For some, hell becomes a way of saying, “They may have hurt me here on earth, but one day, my God will make them suffer far worse —forever!”

But that's not grace. Punishing the wicked doesn’t bring back the innocent whose lives were lost. No matter how severe the consequences, they cannot restore what the wrongdoers have taken away. How would torturing a million Germans bring my lost Jewish family members back to me? Only the true Gospel offers genuine hope—not endless retribution, but the restoration of all things—l will get to see them again!

Eternal Conscious Torment provides a sense of emotional satisfaction rooted in a revenge fantasy disguised with religious rhetoric. It allows people to hold onto bitterness while feeling righteous about it. Instead of confronting the hard work of forgiveness, healing, and grace, Eternal Conscious Torment gives them a theology that says infinite punishment is justice for those who've hurt them.
But this is not the heart of God revealed in Jesus. It is the projection of our pain onto the divine, creating a god in our own broken image.

No amount of revenge will ever bring back a lost loved one. The eternal torment of others cannot undo your grief or heal your broken heart. If you've lost someone, no amount of revenge can heal your heart. Only Christ offers something truly redemptive: resurrection of those you've lost! He will raise everyone to life again. Every tear will be wiped away. No more death. No more trauma. No pain will last forever.
The deepest wounds of history will not be ignored—they will be healed and made new. (Revelation 21:5). That's God's grace to us.
Eternal Conscious Torment Fails the Test of Corrective Justice
A loving punishment meant to guide and correct, aiming not to break but to heal and restore.

God's discipline is not born out of rage, but out of love—a refining fire. True punishment is not about infinite vengeance, but about correction, healing, and restoration. Like a good Father, God disciplines His children not to break them, but to bring them back—whole, humble, and transformed.

However, Eternal Conscious Torment serves no redemptive purpose. It doesn't teach, restore, reconcile, or bring justice. It doesn’t educate or discipline. It is cruelty for cruelty's sake. The hellfire doctrine reduces the Augustinian-Calvinistic god to a sadistic psychopath who delights in the meaningless suffering of others—a doctrine that numbs many Christians’ sense of empathy.

Consider this: most of humanity is shaped from birth by cultural indoctrination. People often sin out of fear, weakness, ignorance, trauma, survival, mental illness, or flawed perceptions. It is their sin that needs to be eliminated—not them!

A true Christian heart should ache at the thought of God eternally tormenting most of humanity. Yet many in the West passionately defend this grotesque doctrine with a distorted, Romanized view of justice. Test your own heart: If you find yourself clinging to the idea that unending suffering is somehow “righteous,” then your understanding of God's justice is severely warped.

In the Hebrew Scriptures,�111 fire is often used to describe God's justice—not as a tool of sadism, but as a force of refinement and purification. Fire refines gold, burns away impurities, and prepares something to be made new. In this context, divine fire isn't about perpetual abuse—it's about healing what's broken, cleansing what's defiled, and restoring what's been lost:
! will put them into the fire; I will refine them like silver and test them like gold. They will call on my name, and I will answer them; I will say,
"They are my people,” and they will say, "The LORD is our God.” (Zechariah 13:9)

Infinite punishment for finite sins is neither just nor merciful. A crime committed in a human lifespan cannot deserve infinite, unending torture—that is not justice; it is sadism. The Augustinian-Calvinist hellfire overrides not only redemptive justice but also grace and mercy entirely—for they mean the offering of redemption, restoration, and forgiveness to the undeserving.

On the other hand, a temporary judgment serves a purpose. And if that purpose is not sadistic but loving—then by simple logic it must be restorative. Any punishment that comes to an end implies that something has been accomplished: purification, repentance, healing, or transformation. Therefore, even those who undergo judgment will ultimately be restored, because a finite correction can only make sense if it leads to a greater good. That's true, restorative justice.
This is not sentimentality—it's biblical logic grounded in the nature of God:
His anger lasts only a moment, but His favor lasts a lifetime. (Psalm 30:5)
For no one is cast off by the Lord forever. Though he brings grief, he will show compassion, so great is his unfailing love. {Lamentations 3:31-32)

The doctrine of Eternal Conscious Torment has nothing to do with God's justice. God's discipline is not unending, and His justice is always intertwined with His love. If hell has an end, its purpose is not to indulge a psychopath’s sadistic desire for revenge, but to bring about redemptive justice. Torturing someone forever— even when disguised in religious language and framed as "doctrine"—doesn’t make anything right; it's simply the product of a sadist’s imagination.

Gladly, some ancient theologians, like St. Isaac the Syrian, grasped this truth: “Those who are tormented in hell are tormented by the invasion of love... It is absurd to assume that the sinners in hell are deprived of God's love."�112

Early Church Fathers of the first and second centuries—among them the theologian, St. Clement of Alexandria—held that because the image of God is present in every human being, all people will ultimately be restored to God. This restoration, however, was not imagined as cheap or automatic; it involved a purifying process by which sin is stripped away from what God created good.

This hopeful view of universal restoration prevailed throughout the first three centuries, lasting until the time of Augustine. The belief was that God’s redemptive work in Christ would ultimately heal, restore, and reconcile all people, bringing the entire creation back into harmony with God like it was before the fall.

To deny such a hope would imply that God condemns His own image—that He consigns to endless ruin what bears His likeness. In other words, it would mean God condemns, forever, something of Himself that He placed within every person.
Conclusion

In the end, the question is not how far God is willing to punish, but how far His love is willing to go. The God revealed in Jesus does not save by fear, nor rule by terror, but heals by truth, patience, and mercy that refuses to let go. Hope is not naive—it is faithful to the character of God. And if love is stronger than death, wiser than wrath, and more enduring than sin, then the story of humanity does not end in despair, but in restoration, light, and a grace vast enough to bring every lost thing home.

chapters.title: Why "Free Will" Can't Justify Eternal Conscious Torment

blocks.s: For centuries, the Augustinian-Calvinist interpretation of hell, known as Eternal Conscious Torment, has been defended on the grounds of free will. The popular argument goes something like this: “God doesn’t send people to hell; they choose it by rejecting Him.” But is this really a choice? Or is it actually the worst form of coercion? If free will is exercised under the threat of unending torment, then it is not free at all. A choice made under existential fear is a forced choice, no different from someone pressing a gun to your head and ordering you to your knees—or an abuser telling their captive, “If you don’t love me, I'll burn you—but it’s your choice.”
Is God Like a Father Warning His Child of the Danger on the Highway?

I have heard others object, saying we're like toddlers playing on a busy highway, and our Father warns us not to run into traffic because we'll get hit. According to this scenario, God warns us, but leaves the decision to us—free will.

But let's press into that fable a little further: What kind of parent lets toddlers play next to a highway in the first place? Any decent, loving parent would build a fence, lock the doors, hold their child's hand, or remove the danger entirely—not step back, warn them once, and then say, “If you get hit, that’s on you!”

If God is truly loving and all-powerful, then placing “spiritually helpless children” near a deadly, infinite consequence—and then holding them responsible for not avoiding it—isn’t justice. It’s negligence at best, cruelty at worst.

Millions die without ever reading the Bible, understanding the Gospel, or even hearing the name Jesus in any meaningful way. Are they still toddlers playing on highways? And if so, who put them there?

What loving parent would throw their child into a fire pit or torture them endlessly for failing a theology test? If you, as an imperfect human, wouldn't even consider doing such a thing—how much more can you trust that your perfect, loving Father would never do it either.
The False Choice: Love or Infinite Suffering

Imagine a person being forced to sign a contract with a knife to their throat. Can we honestly say they made a “free” choice? No, they made a choice to avoid suffering. Love has nothing to do with it. That’s exactly what hellfire theology does —it places a gun to the soul and calls it “free will.”

If rejecting God means unending torment, then there is no real alternative—only forced submission. It makes no actual sense to say that God lets people destroy themselves out of respect for their free will. lf God truly loves us, He CMC OPEN wouldn't just watch us destroy ourselves forever in the name of “free will.” Just like a good parent wouldn't let their hurting child walk into fire without stopping her, real love doesn’t abandon—it rescues.

Or worse, imagine a parent saying to their child, “Love me, or I'll make sure you fall into a pit of fire where you will scream in agony forever.” Would we call that parent loving? Would we say the child has genuine free will? Of course not. Because love, by definition, must be freely and unconditionally given—not extorted through terror!

Yet, fundamentalist theology tells us that God, the supposed source of perfect love, presents humanity with the very same ultimatum: "Worship me, or I'll burn you forever!" The mere fact that rejecting God comes with an infinite penalty makes the choice fundamentally illegitimate.
No religious faith that relies on fear of unending punishment can be called just or loving. A choice made under the threat of permanent suffering is not a choice—it's coercion.
Even in the Torah, Punishment Was Never Without End

Even in the Old Testament's “legalistic” Law, the harshest punishment prescribed for severe sins was the death penalty—not perpetual torture. Those who committed grievous crimes were executed, but their punishment was not torturous, nor did it extend beyond this life. It was only a “game over” in this world, not an everlasting torment in the next.

If torment were truly just, wouldn't God have established it in the Torah? Instead, we find a legal system that is remarkably restrained—one that rarely carried out executions at all and insisted on proportional, limited punishments shaped by mercy and restraint. Justice in the Torah is measured, bounded, and humane. Even when execution was prescribed, it was to be swift, not prolonged torment like that practiced by pagan nations. And nowhere in the Law of Moses is there any threat of endless suffering in the afterlife.

Moreover, history shows us that many individuals who committed grievous sins deserving of death—like Moses (who murdered an Egyptian), King David (who arranged a murder}, and Paul the Apostle (who persecuted Christians)—all found redemption and are now seen as saints in heaven. And if God's justice graciously allowed for redemption even after severe sins, why would He suddenly become more punitive and unforgiving in the afterlife?
Human free will—our stupidity and stubbornness—is not an excuse to condemn us to eternal torment, but rather a reason to transform us.
Fear-Based Love Is Not Love At All

The Bible repeatedly tells us that “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Yet, eternal conscious torment depends and thrives on fear. The entire premise of hellfire theology is rooted in existential terror, not love.

What kind of love demands threats of perpetual torture? If God truly desires a loving relationship with us, why would He construct a system where fear is the primary motivator? An affection given under the threat of hellfire is not love at all— it's survival at best.
Free will without true alternatives is meaningless.
How Free Is Our Mind, Anyway?

For God's judgment to be completely just, our minds would have to be totally and genuinely free—unbiased, unclouded, unaffected by anything or anyone. But that is impossible for us. We are shaped by every experience, every influence, every wound, every fear, every voice that has ever spoken into our lives—even demonic ones. Human beings cannot achieve perfect objectivity or perfect clarity. Only God can. We live in an era where ideas are traded like currency—endless controversial paragraphs scrolling through social media feeds and podcasts. Culture encourages us to “think out loud,” to share reactions freely and boldly, to broadcast interpretations and flood the world with personal and collective opinions. Yet how many of these thoughts and feelings truly belong to us? Psychologist Jordan Peterson often cites psychiatrist Carl Jung's observation: “People don’t have ideas—ideas have people.” According to Peterson, 95% of what we think and say doesn't originate from our true selves. Most of what runs through our minds comes from thought and emotional patterns implanted from the outside. It’s the voice of the world—not our own. When we think, feel, or say “we,” it’s often someone else’s voice speaking through us:

Most of what you think and most of what you say are the opinions of other people. There are things you've read and things people have told you. That's a benefit in some ways because you get all those thoughts that other people have spent a long time formulating, but it's a disadvantage in that it's not exactly you.�113
(Jordan Peterson)

If human judgment is this fragile—shaped by wounds we didn’t choose, fears we never asked for, malevolent spiritual forces we cannot control, cultures we didn’t design, ideas that often “have us” more than we have them—then for God to punish anyone with infinite torment would be monstrously unjust. How could a perfectly good God condemn people forever for a will—thoughts and choices—that was never fully their own? For reactions formed by trauma? For beliefs shaped by upbringing, genetics, personality, pressures, or the thousand invisible influences that make us who we are? If our minds are not free in the fullest sense, then no verdict of infinite punishment could ever be fair. Everlasting hellfire would require perfect clarity, perfect freedom, perfect objectivity—and we do not possess these. Only God does. Therefore, if God is truly just, He cannot hold finite, conditioned creatures eternally accountable for decisions made with limited knowledge, limited understanding, limited freedom, and limited agency. The logic is inescapable: a God of perfect justice could not—would not—burn confused, wounded, influence-shaped humans forever.
Eternal Conscious Torment Diminishes the Gospel
If God is truly love, if He is truly merciful and full of grace, then His actions should reflect a love greater than human love—not less. A truly loving God would:
* Offer endless opportunities for reconciliation (Matthew 18:21-22), even in the age-to-come.
• Bring healing, not inflict endless pain (Luke 5:31-32).
• Aim at the restoration of people and the world—not their destruction (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).
* Desire genuine love, not forced compliance (Romans 8:38-39). e Never create a religious system based on terror, coercion, and perpetual suffering (Lamentations 3:31-32).

Love is not something you can force. It must be freely given.�114 C. S. Lewis Telling someone they will burn in hell unless they believe X is the very definition of coercion—and coercion stands in direct opposition to love, because love cannot be forced. For that reason, any “gospel” that adds a term or condition to God's forgiveness is not the gospel at all. Anything that sounds like, “God has forgiven you in Christ, but only if...” or “You are forgiven if...” is a lie.
The gospel is this: through Christ, God has “taken away the sin of the world” John 1:29). No ifs. No buts. Just a period.
He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world. (1 John 2:2)

God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting people’s sins against them. And he has committed to us the message of reconciliation.
(2 Corinthians 5:18-19)
Conclusion

If Christianity is to reflect the God of love, then it must abandon the abusive framework of the Augustinian-Calvinist hellfire and embrace the true God of Israel as portrayed by Jesus’s transformative power of grace.

God will force no one into submission. He is both wise enough and loving enough that, ultimately, every person will come to that conclusion freely. Right now, we see only a tiny percentage of the full picture. But when the whole truth is finally revealed, no knee will remain unbowed.

Jesus will ultimately gather every soul—no matter how far we've veered off course, no matter how often we've tumbled into ravines of stubbornness, fear, or pain. No matter how prodigal we have become. Through Christ, God will find us, bandage our wounds, and guide us back onto the path, even if it means walking with us through seasons of deep regret, “gnashing of teeth,” and long, dark nights of resistance. Some will fight against the rescue, clinging to their bitterness or confusion. But in the end, no heart will withstand the warmth and relentless virtue of perfect love forever.

When all the illusions melt away, once every trauma is healed, every soul will awaken to the breathtaking summit of truth: Jesus Christ is the unwavering love of God reaching out to find us. No fall is ever too deep. No detour is ever beyond His reach. In the end, and only God knows how, all will find themselves—sometimes battered, always beloved—safely gathered into His embrace.
If your theology portrays God as less loving or caring than the parent you aspire to be, it’s time to rethink that theology.

chapters.title: He Truly Sees Us—Understanding Is Love

blocks.s: My Jewish mother refuses to accept Jesus—not out of rebellion or hardness of heart, but because the “Jesus” presented to her family was clothed in antisemitism and hatred. To her, to her parents, and to her relatives, this so-called Messiah was inseparable from those who claimed His name while persecuting Jews: crusaders, inquisitors, pogroms, blood libels, and ultimately the Nazis.

Before moving to Israel, she grew up in Eastern Europe and endured intense antisemitism from the surrounding Christians, who made sure she knew she was being mocked and bullied solely because she was Jewish.

And if that wasn’t enough, when she later met Messianic believers in Israel, they told her that the same god in whose name her family had been persecuted—the one she was supposed to trust—was now also cruelly burning them in hellfire, just like
Hitler did to them, only this time for good.
Does God Ignore Christian Antisemitism?

When public figures like Candace Owens spread antisemitism day after day—doing so beneath a visible cross and while calling herself Christian—what do you think Jewish people conclude about Christians? About Christ Himself? The message they receive is not love, mercy, or truth, but hostility baptized in religious symbols. And once again, the name of Jesus is dragged through the mud by those who claim to speak for Him.

And now ask yourself—is God really so narrow-minded, so limited in His understanding, empathy, and love, that He would refuse to welcome Jews like my mother into His kingdom simply because the only Jesus they ever met was a distorted, hateful counterfeit?

What kind of justice is that, and what sort of ruthless judge do we imagine Him to be? Where are the mercy, the understanding, and the grace that evangelists so often emphasize? Are they merely concepts in theory or just words in worship songs?

The notion that a God of infinite wisdom, justice, love, power, and understanding would fail to save most of humanity—and instead condemn creatures of such limited rationality and overwhelming emotion to eternal conscious torment—is not just troubling; it is incoherent. To suggest that God would allow people to damn themselves because of misunderstanding, delusion, trauma, pain, fear, or anger— conditions bound up with the very way they were created—portrays Him as distant, indifferent, and blind to the human condition.
Such a god does not truly see us. He does not understand us. And he bears little resemblance to the God revealed in Jesus.
Does God Ignore Christian Bigotry and Sectarianism?
What the Jewish people experienced isn't an isolated case.

The leadership of the British Empire was almost exclusively Christian, and behind the scenes, Christianity played a significant role in shaping the empire and its vision. India was under British occupation for nearly two centuries—and while I don't believe colonial rule is in itself evil, the British Empire was often oppressive, violent, and merciless in its treatment of native populations.

Now ask yourself: what impression has that left in the minds of the one billion Hindus for the past 80 years about what Christianity stands for? When the "Christian nation" ruled with injustice, how would the average Indian raised in Hinduism come to view the Christian God? Likely not as a God of mercy, compassion, and love. Would they then want to follow a Western religion? I very much doubt it.

Now imagine a 15-year-old Hindu girl in the 1800s who dies “without Christ,” having never truly encountered Jesus apart from a distorted version associated with the oppression she and her family endured.
Would a just and loving God disregard her entire life's context and cast such a soul into eternal conscious torment simply for not believing correctly?

If so, then God is not a righteous judge—because a good Judge always seeks understanding and considers context. He weighs motive, background, trauma, and exposure. He understands how culture shapes belief, how history distorts truth, and how human hearts are formed.
To ignore all that would be to render judgment without mercy, justice without wisdom—something no good judge ever does.
And God is not just a good judge—He is the perfect and most merciful judge:
Therefore the Lord waits to be gracious to you; therefore he will rise up to show mercy to you. For the Lord is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him.
(Isaiah 30:18)
Who Are They Truly Rejecting?

We are all shaped by extremely limited knowledge, flawed understanding, emotional wounds, cultural conditioning, religious distortion, and environmental influence. A child born in North Korea or a teen raised in a spiritually abusive Christian household aren't necessarily rejecting God—they’re rejecting what they've been told He is. They may be rejecting a god of terror, control, tribalism, hypocrisy, or injustice. But the true and living God—the Father revealed in Jesus—is often hidden from them. So, is it really rejection if they've never truly encountered Him, understood Him, grasped His message, or known Him? Remember, the very reason Jesus asked the Father to forgive His enemies was because "they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34).
Human consciousness is limited, conditioned, shaped, and often distorted—and it's in that very gap where the grace of God is needed and where it appears, not to condemn, but to forgive.

We are all still in the fog, still sorting through shadows, lies, traumas, and halftruths. Many Christians project a smug sense of certainty, as if they alone—unlike the other 48,999 views—have finally “figured it all out.” But once pressed, even the most respected theologians, priests, rabbis, and mystics have admitted to me in countless theological discussions that their understanding is incomplete on so many topics.

Even the apostle Paul—who experienced visions and revelations—said, “Now we see through a glass, dimly... now I know in part” (1 Corinthians 13:12). If that was true for Paul, how much more so for the rest of us?

And if salvation is to come to the knowledge of Him, then that knowledge— by Paul's own admission—is still partial, indirect, and incomplete: seen “through a glass,” and only “dimly.” Thus, it could be argued that rejection based on a partial or distorted understanding isn’t rebellion—it’s confusion. And God understands it.
I believe this logic applies both to those who pervert His name and image and those who “willfully” reject Him.

I also think that’s why Scripture prophesies that “every knee will bow... every tongue will confess” (Philippians 2:10-11). Not because they are forced to, but because when they finally understand, when the veil is lifted and the truth of God’s goodness is fully revealed, awe and surrender will be the only natural response. Every knee will bow.
When the blinders are gone, when the distortions are burned away by perfect love, then—and only then—will the human soul truly choose. And when it sees God for who He truly is, it will not walk away.

This is why all rejection of God must be temporary. This is why Hell—however one defines it—must also be temporary. Because the rejection is not of God Himself, but of a false image—a distortion. God’s plan is not to punish the confused, the brainwashed by the devil, the indoctrinated by sin, but to enlighten them. And once they are enlightened—truly, fully, gloriously—they will fall to their knees, not in shame or fear, but in praise.
Every knee will bow when every mind truly understands.

chapters.title: God Understands Evil—and the Way It Shapes Us

blocks.s: N o child is born a hater; no baby longs to murder. It is only through trauma and indoctrination in hatred that innocent hearts are twisted into instruments of violence. Boy Named Ahmed—An Illustration

From the moment Ahmed was born, his world was filled with the passionate voices of the muezzins echoing from loudspeakers. Before he could walk the streets of Gaza, his ears had already absorbed words heavy with meaning: Shahid, Jihad, evil Zionists, martyrdom, and being told Allah is the God of revenge.

At three years old, Ahmed was already chanting hateful phrases he didn’t understand but was praised for saying. His uncle placed a toy gun in his hand and told him he was Allah's lion against the Jews. “Allah will reward you. One day, you will bring honor to your family,” he said.

His picture books weren't like those of Western children. They were filled with tales of young boys who died fighting the so-called “enemy"—Jews portrayed not as individuals, but as one cursed people, dehumanized and imagined with horns. In one story, a Jewish man betrayed the Prophet and was justly punished. In another, a teenager’s soul was lifted to paradise because he threw a stone at a Jew and was killed. Ahmed learned that paradise was closest to the brave, and bravery meant resistance, and resistance meant bloodshed.

At five, Ahmed sat cross-legged in the mosque, where the imam taught that to fight the Jews was not only political—it was divine will. The Quran was quoted to him in fragments, always ending in certainty: “You, little one, are chosen by Allah to resist. To fight is to believe.”

By age seven, Ahmed was playing “ambush” with his cousins in alleyways, pretending to sneak up on Jews made of cardboard. He practiced knife grips, praised by his older brother, who had photos of armed martyrs on his bedroom wall. At family dinners, the name of a man who had blown himself up at a Jerusalem bakery was mentioned with pride. “He is in paradise,” his aunt said, “and now his whole family is honored.”

Ahmed didn’t learn Hebrew. He didn’t meet Jewish children. He didn’t hear stories about peace or shared pain. He only knew what he had been indoctrinated with: fear, resistance, and the promise that Allah's favor would rest on him if he fought unto death.
By thirteen, driven by sexual desire and swayed by warped beliefs, he was led to believe he'd be rewarded with 72 virgins if he died committing violence against Jews and Christians.

By fifteen, Anmed was ready. He no longer smiled when he played. His play had become preparation. When a recruiter from a militant group noticed him at the mosque, he praised his knowledge, his devotion, and his seriousness. “You are pure,” the man said. “The world haven't corrupted you. You are now ready. You will make Allah proud!” Ahmed believed him.

The boy who once held a toy gun now held a real one. He no longer saw the world in shades—only in black and white. Us and them. Allah and the cursed Jews. He was told that if he died fighting, he would awaken immediately after in the gardens of paradise, with angels and virgin girls attending to him, and countless heavenly rewards awaiting.
He didn't know the faces of the people he was taught to hate. He never met them. He only knew the story he had been told, over and over again, in the name of Allah. He didn't know better.

This story might sound like fiction to a Western “enlightened” ear, but it’s an everyday reality in parts of the Middle East and Africa, where groups such as Hamas, Hezbollah, ISIS, Boko Haram, and Islamic Jihad have often used brainwashed children as soldiers. Child soldiering is evil at its worst—these kids were never truly given a chance, certainly not like a “pastor’s kid" born into a Christian family in Texas.
We Don’t Realize What We Don’t Know

By definition, the human mind is incapable of grasping all truth, because we are not all-knowing. From birth, we are slowly formed—often unconsciously—by inherited narratives. We do choose freely, but our freedom is never absolute; it is always heavily conditioned.

And this is where I believe God’s understanding and mercy come into play. I’m not suggesting young terrorists are in for a garden of roses, but God is not binary. Divine justice isn't a simple equation of bliss versus torment.

Being refined and purified by fire is hardly what one would picture a pleasant experience, but losing reward or facing consequences for wrongdoing doesn’t have to mean endless torment in hellfire, as some Christian (and Islamic) traditions claim. Besides, if all will ultimately be resorted, then even the most tragic and violent deaths are not the final word. Every person—whether lost traumatically or naturally—will be resurrected and restored again. In that light, even the worst death becomes a temporary condition, not an everlasting one.
If God's grace isn’t bigger than our own, then it’s not really divine grace at all.
We Wrestle Not Against Flesh and Blood

There is a dimension of evil that is often ignored—one reflected in struggles like Ahmed’s—which I believe God understands far more deeply than we do and fully takes into account. It is not only culture that shapes human beings; spiritual forces are at work as well. And humans, fragile and impressionable as we are, are profoundly susceptible to the influence and damage of these dark powers.

The biblical assertion that “we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places” (Ephesians 6:12) highlights that the true nature of our struggles is spiritual rather than human. In this view, dark spiritual forces lurk behind every terrorist and murderer, pulling their strings like marionettes—whether figuratively or perhaps even literally (demonic possession).

These dark spiritual forces influence everything—from global systems down to individual lives. And make no mistake: Satan targets the Church as well. He attacks its beliefs, its doctrines, its Bible translations, its commentaries, and its teachings. How else can we explain the sheer number of conflicting theologies within Christianity, some of which are so distorted and grotesquely unlike the character of God that they could only arise from spiritual deception rather than divine truth?

All of creation is engaged in a spiritual battle and influenced by powerful spiritual forces. Most human beings are not even aware that they are caught up in a cosmic spiritual struggle. But since our struggle is spiritual in essence and universal in scope, then the solution—the salvation and redemption of humanity—must be universal as well. The universality of the conflict demands a universality of redemption, revealing a God whose saving grace is as far-reaching as the battle itself, and not confined by the limits of human awareness, wisdom, or understanding.

And if the primary conflict truly lies between spiritual forces far more powerful than we are, then human beings are not inherently evil, but image-bearers under assault —wounded and influenced by evil. In that case, God's task is not to eliminate sinners, but to eradicate sin itself. The victory over these powers must therefore resemble healing a disease—not killing the patient, but destroying the infection.

If Christ truly accomplished that—atoning for the world so that, in the end, all are saved—then what we see is a complete and unambiguous victory over the powers of evil, leaving them with nothing. It proclaims that God’s power and love are so vast that they ultimately redeem not merely a few, but all of creation from the grip of these spiritual adversaries, not leaving even a single one behind.
Conclusion

God's desire that “all people be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4) becomes a reflection of His omnipotent capability to defeat the true enemies—sin and evil—not the individuals influenced by them.

Just as evil and death do not discriminate in their reach, neither does God's salvation. His redemptive love encompasses ail, ensuring that every soul is eventually restored. This reflects the character of a God who does not abandon His creation to ruin, but rescues it fully—revealing both His supreme authority and power, and His limitless mercy.

When we finally see the story as God sees it—when we understand that evil is deeper than individuals and salvation wider than our categories—we discover that God’s answer to darkness is not abandonment or torment, but redemption. His justice does not end in exclusion, but in healing; not in destruction, but in restoration. Sin and evil are confronted, judged, and undone, yet the image-bearer is never discarded. This is the triumph of the gospel: not that a few escape while the rest are lost, but that light overcomes darkness, truth dispels deception, and love outlasts every distortion. A world apart from God fractures and decays, but in Christ, what was lost is being found, what was broken is being restored, and what was condemned is being redeemed. The world is not being thrown away—it is being saved!

chapters.title: Love, Fear, and the Conditional "If" - Why the Gospel Cannot Be Rooted in Terror

blocks.s: n religious discussions, few words carry as much weight as “if.” At the center of I much Christian theology stand conditional statements: “If you do or believe X, then Y will happen.” Depending on how that if is understood, it can either open the door to a living, transformative relationship with God—or warp faith into a system of anxiety, insecurity, and fear. The meaning of that “if” depends entirely on the framework through which we read it. And here, two very different theological paradigms emerge:
1, Existential Condition (Fear-Based Theology):
“If you don't intellectually believe the right doctrine or behave a certain way, you'll suffer eternal conscious torment in hell.”
This view dominates much of Western theology. It places salvation on a razor’'s edge, dependent on intellectual or moral precision. In other words, this "if" is a feardriven faith.

I'm very familiar with the verses that speak about "fear of God" (e.g., Proverbs 9:10; 19:23; Matthew 10:28; 2 Corinthians 7:1). However, the commonly translated biblical term "fear," particularly the Hebrew yir and the Greek phobos, does not equate to the modern English understanding of terror or fright, but instead primarily signifies awe, reverence, and profound respect toward God. Distinct Hebrew words exist for the feeling of terror or dread, such as pachad and eimah.
2. Relational/Consequential Condition (Love-Based Theology):

If my son misbehaved and refused to repent, I might deny him ice cream—a temporary consequence that affects our relationship. But I would never even consider taking his life simply because he refused to repent. In other words, the “if” shapes the quality of relationship and the consequences within it—not the child's existence or ultimate destiny.

This understanding—deeply rooted in Jewish thought—views God not as a tyrant seeking perpetual punishment, but as a loving Father who disciplines yet never abandons. This is the consistent pattern of God's relationship with Israel throughout the Hebrew Scriptures.
Even at Israel’s lowest moments—idolatry, rebellion, exile—God's promise remained unwavering:
! will not reject them or abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them; for I am the Lord their God. {Leviticus 26:44—45)

This is what the Lord says, he who appoints the sun to shine by day, who decrees the moon and stars to shine by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar—the Lord Almighty is his name: “Only if these decrees vanish from my sight,” declares the Lord, “will Israel ever cease being a nation before me.”
(Jeremiah 31:35-36)
If this is God's love toward a rebellious, “stiff-necked" (Exodus 32:9; Deuteronomy 9:6, 13) and chronically unfaithful (Jeremiah 3:20; 32:33) people, does it not apply to us as well?

These verses echo a central biblical truth: God corrects, but He does not cast off forever. His judgments are restorative, not annihilating. He doesn’t engage in cancel culture because His steadfast love remains constant, even when His people fall short.
The God who refused to forsake Israel in her rebellion will not forsake us either. His love for His creation endures even when ours does not, and His faithfulness remains even when ours falters.

The gospel is not a fragile contract that collapses at the first sign of human weakness. It is a relationship—covenantal, parental, rooted in fidelity rather than fear. God disciplines to heal, not to destroy; to guide, not to damn.
As I was writing these very lines, I received a short email, and due to its ironic timing,
I decided to take it as a “divine sign” and include it in the book:

Hi. Do you have a link or a book that talks about headcovering? I come from a Mennonite community, and goodness, they go so far that, if I don't have a headband, I'll be lost forever. That 1 Corinthians 11,13, 15 is a straight command from God.
Thank you for all your work and Shalom.

You see, if our motivation comes from fear instead of love, insecurity and anxiety will slowly creep into our souls, because we can never truly be certain that God won't punish us forever for not believing the right thing or behaving the right way.
When “If” Becomes a Threat Instead of an Invitation

If unending torture is held out as a conditional threat—based on performance or possessing the “right” faith—then the gospel is reduced to a transaction. Fear becomes the engine. Obedience is no longer born of love, but of terror. “I'll believe— just promise You won't torture me forever.”
Unless one is Hannibal Lecter or the bogeyman, by any honest standard of logic, that is not love. It is coercion.
This is why the apostle John wrote:
There is no fear in love. But perfect love casts out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. (1 John 4:18)

A relationship with God built on fear cannot be intimate. You cannot draw near to someone you're afraid might destroy you for one reason or another. The soul becomes obsessed with getting the formula right—never resting, never sure, never free.

In fact, research shows that Scrupulosity and OCD are disproportionately high among fundamentalist Christians. A 2019 study, for example, found that the severity of OCD symptoms linked to scrupulosity differed between religious groups, with conservative Catholics and Protestants reporting the highest levels.�115

If you're part of this group, please let me encourage you: No matter how far you fall, you cannot outpace the love of God. No matter how badly you stumble, you can never outdo God in love or forgiveness. You will never be better at sinning than He is at redeeming.

If God is truly infinite and never changes, so are His mercy and grace everlasting. Thus, by definition, our capacity to sin can never exceed His power to redeem. To believe otherwise is to imagine that human failure can outmatch divine compassion. But that would make our sin stronger than God's grace—an impossibility. No matter the depth of your stumbling, His forgiveness will always reach deeper still.
The "if" of Divine Love

A faith rooted in love looks very different from one rooted in fear. Love leads to intimacy, joy, and a life of gratitude. Fear leads to anxiety, legalism, and performancedriven spirituality. When we fear God's rejection, we become actors on a stage, hoping our performance will earn divine applause. But when we trust God’s acceptance, we become children in the arms of a Father—free to grow, learn, stumble, and rise again.
God's “if” isn’t about whether you'll be endlessly forgiven or endlessly tormented— but about the consequences and rewards that flow from how you live this life.
Scripture is full of consequences—not eternal condemnation, but consequences nonetheless. Paul says:
Each one’s work will become manifest... and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. (1 Corinthians 3:13)
We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ... to receive what is due for what he has done in the body. (2 Corinthians 5:10)

In this light, the “if” is no longer existential—it mainly shapes the status and rewards in the age to come. The judgment is not about sadistic wrath or punishment for its own sake, but refinement and purification. Just as a loving parent might discipline a child without ever withdrawing love or identity, so too God punishes for the sake of correction.

The outcome? Not annihilation. Not everlasting hellfire. But loss—or gain—of reward, honor, and role in God's coming Kingdom. Just like a good parent disciplines but never disowns, God corrects without rejecting (Hebrews 12:6).

This distinction is crucial. If the “if” relates to our identity, inclusion, or immortality itself, then we live in constant dread. But if it relates to our calling, responsibility, and future reward, then it becomes a path to growth.
That’s the Gospel. Not “God threatened us into heaven,” but “God loved us into transformation.”

God still disciplines. There are still stakes. But God's corrections are born of love, not hate. Like a physician cutting out disease—not to punish, but to heal. Like a fire that refines gold—not to destroy, but to purify.
Reclaiming the “If” as a Blessing

When we see the “if" in the right light, it turns into a medal, a trophy, a bokeh, a promise—not an existential threat. It calls us not to fear never-ending damnation, but to live with purpose. To win heavenly rewards. To reflect God. To steward our gifts. To store up treasures in heaven. To become Christlike. Every act of love, every sacrifice, every act of mercy—none of it is forgotten.

In this light, the “if’ becomes a potential blessing, not a burden and threat. It challenges us, but never threatens what Christ did for us. It corrects us, but never condemns us. It sharpens our purpose without undermining our identity.

Any discipline that proceeds from a loving source must serve a loving purpose. By simple logic, that purpose can only be restorative. God's judgment, then, is not vindictive fury but the fierce fire of His love—burning away what destroys, cleansing what corrupts, purging what enslaves.
Judgement that comes to an end implies that something has been achieved: purification, transformation, repentance. And if repentance is reached, then restoration necessarily follows.
Conclusion

Let us, then, walk not in existential fear, but in awe of the grace that welcomes us. Let us believe not for the sake of escaping, but to reflect the One who saves us in every way. For perfect love drives out fear—and draws us deeper into the joy of the Father's heart.

Let us reject the existential dread masquerading as theology, and embrace the love that drives out fear. Let us obey not because we are terrified, but because we are loved. Let us remember: We are not being threatened into faith. We are being invited into glory.

The retributive vision of eternal conscious torment portrays God as fragile, wounded, capricious, and vindictive—seeking to pacify Himself through the suffering of others. It imagines an offended ruler who lashes out, rather than a healer who restores. But if God truly is love, then His response must be compassion: to heal, not to harm; to restore, not to destroy. Eternal conscious torment is irreconcilable with a God who is love—good, perfect, self-sufficient, and complete in Himself.

I ‘m often amazed at how some Christians use Hitler as the ultimate example of evil—and rightly so, given that he burned countless people alive—yet simultaneously attribute to God the very same actions and character they condemn in Hitler:

If only born-again Christians go to heaven, then the piles of suitcases and bags of human hair displayed at the Holocaust Museum represent thousands upon thousands of men, women, and children suffering eternal agony at the hands of an angry God. 1
(Rachel Held Evans)

The logic used to defend eternal conscious torment for someone like Hitler does not stop with him. It inevitably extends to the six million Jewish men, women, and children he murdered—most of whom were not believers in Jesus—and condemns them to the very same fate. Under this framework, victims and perpetrators alike, the murdered and the Nazi murderers, end up suffering identical punishment: endless torment.
That conclusion alone exposes the moral bankruptcy of the system

Think about how absurd this is: under the ECT view, some of the kindest people who ever lived would endure endless torment just like the most monstrous figures in history. And that, we are told, is God's justice?
Preaching God's Name in Vain

Someone has said that no theology is worth believing that cannot be preached standing in front of the gates of Auschwitz. I, for one, could not stand at those gates and preach a version of God's sovereignty that makes the extermination of six million Jews, including many children, a part of the will and plan of God such that God foreordained and rendered it certain.�117
(Roger Olson, PhD)

If a “gospel” becomes morally grotesque and collapses into incoherence in the face of atrocities like the Holocaust, then it is not the “good news of great joy for all people” (Luke 2:10). It is a theological system in desperate need of reexamination.

A true gospel—if it is truly good—must be able to speak meaningfully into humanity's darkest hours, offering a hope deeper than despair and a compassion strong enough to touch the wounds of history. If our theology becomes useless, or even cruel, when placed beside the worst horrors humanity has endured, then perhaps the problem is not with God—but with the way we have come to understand Him.
Hitler’s Final Moments

It’s one thing for people to have never heard of Jesus or to have only encountered a distorted image of Him, but what about those who are truly evil? What name comes to mind when you think of someone you could never imagine in heaven? For me, growing up as a descendant of Holocaust survivors, that name was Hitler—the monstrous German dictator responsible for millions of deaths, including members of my own Jewish family. Adolf Hitler, who ended his life by gunshot on April 30, 1945, in his Fihrerbunker in Berlin, embodied for many the very definition of irredeemable evil.
But there’s an overlooked part of Hitler's story that turns our assumptions on their head.

During Hitler’s meteoric rise to power, a German theologian named Dietrich Bonhoeffer became one of his fiercest critics—eventually participating in a plot to overthrow the Nazi regime. For this, Bonhoeffer was arrested, imprisoned, and finally executed in April 1945, just days before Germany's defeat. His letters and papers from prison, published posthumously, remain one of the most profound testimonies to Christian conviction under tyranny.

According to a report online, a letter was found hidden deep within the ruins of Hitler's bunker. This letter, allegedly written shortly before his suicide, revealed something shocking: Hitler had been haunted by Bonhoeffer’s teachings in the final months of the war. The words he had once dismissed as weakness now gnawed at him. His letter records overwhelming remorse for his crimes, particularly against the Jewish people. It describes a desperate cry for God’s mercy—a confession, a plea.

The Soviet propaganda machine, it is said, suppressed the letter. Allowing Hitler even the possibility of redemption would have undermined the black-and-white narrative. Hitler, in their view, could only be seen as monstrous and damned—not complex, not broken, not redeemable.
And yet, this possibility forces us to ask a deeper question:
What if he did repent? What if, in the last moments of his life, Adolf Hitler sincerely sought forgiveness from Christ?

Many Christians—especially within “born again” and Calvinist traditions—see no serious theological problem with granting salvation to someone evil—even Hitler— provided he repented moments before death, much like the thief crucified beside Jesus. In this framework, a sincere last-second prayer or “inviting Jesus into one’s heart” is enough to secure salvation, regardless of a lifetime of atrocities.
The irony is chilling. Under this logic, the six million Jews Hitler murdered would suffer eternal conscious torment, while Hitler himself would walk free.
Think about that for a moment.
According to this belief, the murderer is embraced while the murdered are forever tortured.
The abuser finds peace while those he abused find everlasting agony.
The "born again" oppressor is granted heaven, while his victims suffer permanent torment in hellfire.

But strangely, these same Christians erupt into spiritual outrage at even the possibility that repentance could be accepted and salvation granted if it occurred five seconds after death—when a soul finally sees undiluted reality face-to-face. In that case, they declare, it is "too late"—grace is cut off, God becomes a cosmic executioner, and the door to heaven is slammed forever.

How strange—how different the outcome, all because of ten seconds. Had Hitler whispered a prayer for mercy five seconds before death, many would eagerly welcome him into heaven. But had that same repentance occurred five seconds after his final breath—after facing pure truth—most would declare it impossible. As if the ticking of a clock, not the sincerity of the heart, determines the fate of an eternal soul. How fragile, how arbitrary, Western theology can be.
If this strikes you as not just logically contradictory but also morally disturbing, you're definitely not alone.

The theology that flows from Augustine and Calvin, with its binary afterlife of instant heaven or endless hell, demands such contradictions. It forces you to celebrate Hitler's "salvation" (if he repented) while condemning Anne Frank to endless burning —because inherited belief systems, not moral sanity, is running the show.
And yet, Scripture reveals a better, more coherent story—a story of justice that restores, not simply punishes; of mercy that outlasts death; of love that never fails (1 Corinthians 13:8).

The tale of Hitler's letter circulates on the internet, yet it has never been definitively verified. In any case, whether this letter is real or not is ultimately beside the point. The story is a thought exercise—an exploration of how deeply the Gospel challenges our assumptions about justice, mercy, and human worth.
“Where Sin Increased, Grace Increased All the More" (Romans 5:20)

Salvation is not an on-off switch. It is not a mechanical transaction triggered by the correct words spoken at the last second of life. And though it is not easy for me to say this as a Jew, I believe God's mercy and compassion are far greater than my own. His love extends even to my greatest enemies.

I would rather see Hitler—and any other deeply wicked person—come to the knowledge of the truth, repent, bow the knee, and confess Jesus Christ as Lord, than be tortured forever for no redemptive purpose. Endless torment accomplishes nothing. Repentance does.

Yes, even a soul as dark and twisted as Hitler’s could, through a hell-like process of judgment and purification, truly repent and ultimately be restored. That does not minimize evil; it declares the final victory of God over it.

But not cheaply. Not instantly. And certainly not without facing the full weight and horror of what he did. Restoration is never about sweeping evil under the rug. It's about confronting it, being broken by it, and allowing grace—slow, costly, searing grace—to heal what seems beyond repair.

People like Hitler would first have to face hell—the full, unfiltered reality of the harm and suffering they inflicted on others. What that hell looks like, I do not pretend to know. But I imagine it as an encounter with truth so unbearable it can no longer be evaded: seeing their deeds as they truly were, feeling them not abstractly but inwardly, bearing their weight in the depths of the soul until denial collapses and repentance becomes unavoidable.

Such repentance would not erase what was done. It would transform the one who did it. They would not emerge honored or exalted. If anything, they would be “least in the kingdom." Their honor would be stripped away, their rewards forfeited, their former power undone—exchanged for humility, service, and a long apprenticeship in love.
But restoration does not mean denial. Restoration means healing after justice has been satisfied—not human revenge, but God's perfect justice that disciplines to restore, not destroy.

In the end, if Hitler is in heaven, it will not be because his crimes were forgotten. Yesterday was Israel's Holocaust Remembrance Day, and like every year, a nationwide loud siren screamed for two minutes while everyone stood still. We still remember. We still grieve. But no amount of vengeance can bring back our loved ones. And it's okay, because I know they, too, will see God, will meet Jesus, and will come to accept Him. If they too are to be saved, then all the harm done to them by evil Hitlers was only temporary.

In the end, if Hitler is in heaven, it will be because God's mercy is wider than we dared imagine—and because God's justice is not a mirror of human wrathful vengeance, but a fire that purifies even the worst among us. A fire that burns away the impure and forges what's left into precious gold.
If that scandalizes you, remember: It is not Hitler who defines the limits of God's grace. It is Jesus—the One who said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." (Luke 23:34)
And if He could pray that prayer for the very men nailing Him to the cross, then maybe the scandal of grace is exactly what we need to be confronted with—and transformed by.

chapters.title: Then What's the Point in Evangelizing?

blocks.s: An objection frequently raised is, "If everyone will eventually be redeemed, then why evangelize?"

During an Iranian missile attack in Israel in June 2025, the siren blared and chaos broke out. Everyone rushed for cover, and those on the street dashed into the nearest bomb shelter across from us, desperate to be safe. In the middle of it all, one family grew visibly upset, insisting that only residents from nearby buildings should be let in. They demanded the doors be locked to keep “outsiders” away.

Later, I sat with one of them, who was still visibly upset that "strangers" had sought safety in “their” shelter. I told him I understood the practical limits—sometimes a shelter can be overcrowded and unsafe for all. But in this case, there was still enough space. I sensed this was not a practical concern, but something deeper—an emotional wall. So I asked him, “Don’t you care about these people? What if you closed the door, and they died from the missile strike—how would you feel?” He answered, almost numbly, “I don't feel anything anymore.” I gently pressed, “Why? Did something happen to you in the past?” His eyes instantly filled with tears as he confessed, “I did something terrible when I was young and stupid. Since then, I don’t care because I don't feel anything anymore.”

Now, to those who ask why the gospel should be preached at all if every knee will eventually bow: does the gospel still matter to someone like him? Can the Good News reach a person who feels shattered—hollow, numb, almost dead inside? Can hearing that he is already forgiven in Christ (no ifs) begin to heal a wounded soul? Can the gospel breathe life into a heart that feels like a corpse—or is all it offers merely a ticket to heaven after death?

And what about the Jewish mothers whose children were kidnapped by Hamas on October 7, 2023, and murdered in Gaza? Or the Palestinian mothers who lost their babies? Can the gospel—the announcement that death will not have the final word, that all will be raised and live again—restore even a measure of hope to their broken hearts? Does the promise of reunion, of seeing their loved ones again, matter? Does it heal? Does it sustain?
When the Very Question Exposes the Misunderstanding

Is God really so narrow and selective that the gospel applies only to a small, enlightened few, as many believe? Or is the good news actually good news for all, especially for the grieving, the traumatized, the lost, the searching, and the broken?

But honestly, the very fact that we find ourselves wrestling with this objection reveals just how far the Western gospel has drifted from its original message in the first century. The questions we ask today expose a disconnect between the life-giving, present-tense gospel proclaimed by Jesus and His apostles, and the reduced version many have inherited—a somewhat gnostic gospel preoccupied with the afterlife, rather than transformation here and now.

The point of sharing the gospel is not to "save" people from falling into a fire pit in the afterlife. The gospel is meant to rescue people from the hell they're living in right now. It’s about offering genuine hope to the hurting and direction to the lost. It's about awakening compassion where numbness has taken over, bringing new life where the soul has gone cold. The gospel isn’t just a promise for the future—it's an invitation to be made whole now, to breathe again, to live as we were created to live.
That's why we share it—even if God’s mercy will reach everyone in the end: Because people need to be saved from the hell they already live in, today.
So why should you evangelize?
You evangelize because you want people to truly live and live abundantly.
You evangelize because healed hearts heal others.
You evangelize because forgiven people forgive.
You evangelize because the Prince of Peace has come into the world—and through Him peace can be made even with enemies.
You evangelize because to know Jesus is to overflow with the life He gives—a life that cannot help but spill outward.
You evangelize because you love, and love cannot sit still.
Evangelism is not recruitment into a cosmic survival bunker. It’s an invitation into the healing flood of God's restoration.
We evangelize because we have tasted something beautiful—and beauty demands to be shared.
We evangelize because we have seen the face of love—and love demands to be reflected.
We evangelize because the Kingdom of God is not just something we wait for—it is something we build, one act of kindness, one word of truth, one spark of mercy at a time.
Evangelizing for a Better Society

The beauty of the gospel is that it was never meant to stop at the level of private belief or individual spirituality. From the beginning, its horizon has been public, communal, and even cosmic. Jesus spoke of a kingdom—not merely a personal rescue plan—and Acts tells us that this message was meant to spread outward, reshaping lives, communities, and nations (e.g., Matthew 28:19-20, Mark 16:15, Acts 1:8). Wherever the gospel has taken root in its fullness, it has carried with it a vision of human dignity, moral responsibility, justice tempered by mercy, and the worth of every person made in the image of God.

Now consider the world beyond the West. Have you ever been to Syria, Afghanistan, North Korea, Sudan, Iran, Gaza, or Yemen? These are places scarred by tyranny, endless cycles of violence, suppression of conscience, and the crushing of the weak. This is not a matter of cultural superiority, but of moral contrast. Societies shaped by Judeo-Christian values—however imperfectly—have tended to cultivate ideas that many now take for granted: the sanctity of human life, limits on state power, care for the poor, the dignity of women and children, and the idea that rulers themselves are accountable to a higher moral law.

The gospel challenges injustice not only in hearts but in systems. It confronts cruelty, tribalism, and oppression wherever they appear. It insists that power exists to serve, not to dominate; that truth matters; that love of neighbor is not optional; and that the strong are responsible for the weak. These ideas did not arise naturally in human history—they were seeded, slowly and often painfully, by a worldview rooted in the Hebrew Scriptures and embodied in the life of Jesus.

To say that the gospel is only about personal salvation is to shrink it far below its biblical scope. It is not merely about where an individual goes after death; it is about what happens to the world while we are alive. It is a message meant to humanize societies, restrain evil, inspire compassion, and cultivate justice. When received rightly, it does not erase cultures, but heals them—calling every nation to become more humane, more just, and more aligned with the goodness for which humanity was created.
The gospel, at its best, is not an escape from the world. It is God's invitation to remake it.
But Wouldn't People "Backslide" Without the Threat of Endless Hellfire?

Discipline, loss of rewards, and correction are still unpleasant, even if the punishment is only temporary. But the idea that Christians would "backslide" into terrible behavior without the looming threat of burning forever not only paints a grim picture of God but is also both logically and morally flawed.

Some would argue that preaching hellfire is necessary to demonstrate God's justice. But in the apostolic era, God's justice was demonstrated in Christ's victory over sin, death, and evil—not in the perpetual torment and suffering of souls. God's justice was about setting things right, healing creation, and “reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

If the only thing preventing someone from committing evil is the fear of eternal conscious torment, then we're not talking about righteousness—we’re talking about restraint. That's not transformation; it's just wickedness kept on a leash. Is that what Christianity is all about?

The God of the Hebrew Scriptures doesn’t manipulate with terror—He draws with chesed (lovingkindness). Grounding morality in existential fear undermines the very heart of the Gospel. The teachings and life of Jesus embody this: not a religion of fear, but a way of life rooted in mercy, truth, justice, and love.

True faith is not driven by fear but by love, compassion, and a desire to do what is right. A relationship with God grounded in terror does not foster trust, growth, or genuine devotion. Fear may produce temporary compliance, but it cannot produce love—and love is exactly what God asks of us: “Love the Lord your God... and love your neighbor as yourself” (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18; see also Matthew 22:37-39).
Religion Motivated by Fear vs. Faith Inspired by Love

Take my Jewish friends—religious and secular alike—as an example. Many follow a strong moral and Jewish ethical code, often making sacrifices for complete strangers, giving generously, and working toward justice and peace—all without believing in the doctrine of eternal torment in hellfire. Their lives show that living morally doesn’t depend on the fear of eternal conscious torment.
If your beliefs require the threat of unending punishment to guide your morals, then it is not love that drives your behavior—it is fear. Again, you are simply a malevolent Christian on a leash.
True faith isn’t about avoiding punishment. It's about becoming more like the One who forgives, heals, restores, and loves—even to the end.

As we saw at the beginning of the book, the apostles never evangelized with threats of flames. They preached Jesus—His resurrection, His fulfillment of prophecy, His invitation to repent from idols and receive forgiveness and blessings, and His promise of great rewards and honor in God's restored world for those who are faithful.
Conclusion

Evangelism, then, is not about scaring people into heaven. It is about proclaiming the goodness of God, the beauty of Christ, the power of His resurrection, and the hope of transformation. It is about inviting all people to step into the abundant life God offers here and now—and in the world to come. It’s about proclaiming life over death, healing over brokenness, light over darkness. It’s about inviting people to live the life they were created for—now and forever.
Hellfire was never the driving force of Apostolic evangelism. Life was. And it still should be today.

Healthy theology cannot be built on private visions. It must be grounded in the text—its language, its context, and its coherent witness. My conclusions do not arise from what someone claims to have seen in a vision, during a coma, or after a near-death episode, but from what the biblical authors actually wrote and meant within their Jewish worldview. The foundation of doctrine is not personal experience. It is Scripture.
The Problem with NDE as Authority

Near-death experiences (NDEs) are often presented as compelling evidence for what awaits us beyond death. But there is a serious problem: they contradict one another. Some describe a realm where all people appear healed, joyful, and at peace. Others recount scenes of terror, darkness, and torment. They cannot all be correct. When “experiences and “visions” compete with one another, they cancel each other out. They cannot function as final authority. Scripture, however, does not contradict itself in this way. When Scripture speaks, it stands.
What Science Actually Suggests

Research indicates that in the moments before, during, and immediately after clinical death, the brain undergoes a massive surge of neurotransmitters—dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine among them. This chemical cascade, often part of a terminal spike in brain activity, is believed to contribute to intense experiences: feelings of peace, dread, heightened awareness, or vivid imagery.

Researchers also note that the brain may remain active for at least thirty seconds after the cardiovascular system has ceased functioning. In such a state, it is not unreasonable to assume that pre-existing beliefs about the afterlife shape the structure of the experience itself.
In other words, if someone already expects light and angels, or flames and judgment, the mind under extreme neurological stress may supply imagery consistent with those expectations.

This does not mean people are lying. It means human consciousness is complex, especially at the edge of death. But it does mean such experiences are subjective and cannot serve as doctrinal authority.
Experience Is Not Revelation
As a theologian and Bible scholar, I am not interpreting dreams, visions, or subjective encounters. I am interpreting Scripture.
The Bible—not NDEs, not testimonies, not emotional stories—is the standard. Experiences may be meaningful to individuals, but they are not the measuring rod of truth.
Whenever someone shares a vivid dream or vision of the afterlife, I am reminded of
Jeremiah’s warning:

“Do not listen to what the prophets are prophesying to you; they fill you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the Lord.... I have heard what the prophets say who prophesy lies in my name. They say, ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’ How long will this continue in the hearts of these lying prophets, who prophesy the delusions of their own minds?”
So, bottom line, when it comes to doctrine, I believe it’s best to stick with Scripture rather than personal experience, including NDEs.

f you aim to educate and warn your child about the dangers of hard drugs, it's I logical to do so well in advance rather than during or after they've started using. Similarly, if the concept of Hellfire is as crucial as believed—impacting everyone's eternity—one would expect it to be clearly and prominently communicated from the earliest stages of the biblical text.

However, when we examine the progression of how Hellfire is discussed in biblical texts, there's a notable absence in the places where it might be most expected. This absence raises questions about the clarity and priority given to the concept in the scriptures.

Initially, God warns Adam and Eve only of mortality—no mention of eternal torture of some kind, just a life of toil followed by death. Then, throughout the entire Torah, there is not a single warning of eternal Hellfire.
Concurrently, surrounding pagan cultures have rich mythologies featuring fiery underworlds for the wicked, yet these ideas are not reflected in early Jewish theology or anywhere in the Old Testament.
Life's Purpose Isn't Escapism

The idea sounds audacious, even scandalous. It feels almost unthinkable to imagine offering forgiveness to the very hands that mocked, spat in the face, hammered nails into the flesh, and ultimately crucified Christ.
But what seems offensive and unthinkable to us was not unthinkable to Jesus.
From the cross itself—while still bleeding, still suffocating, still surrounded by hatred—He pleaded:
“Father, forgive them!” (Luke 23:34)

Some might say there’s no forgiveness for those who turn away from Christ. But if Christ could ask the Father to forgive those who committed the very act of killing Him, then surely His love atones for every human heart, no matter how resistant or broken.
God's love is not small.
It is not finite or bound by time.
It is not limited by resistance or human rebellion.
His love is boundless, relentless, and eternal—because He is.
The Gospel was never meant to terrify people into belief.
It was never designed to be a cosmic threat hanging over humanity’s head.
The Gospel is a proclamation of forgiveness and an invitation—into love, into healing, into transformation, into truth, into life.

It is the announcement that God’s goodness is stronger than our darkest failures, that His mercy outlasts our stubbornness, and that His desire and ability to save are far greater than our ability to resist Him.
Hell's "Fire" Meant for Refinement, Cleansing, and Purification

Perhaps the true purpose of what we call “hell”’—metaphorically speaking—is, as several early Church Fathers taught, to encounter God's purifying fire: a refining and healing process rather than mere retribution. Figures such as Origen of Alexandria, Gregory of Nyssa, Clement of Alexandria, and later Isaac of Nineveh (the Syrian) spoke of divine judgment not as endless revenge, but as corrective, medicinal, and ultimately restorative—fire that burns away corruption so that what God created good may finally be made whole.

I don't claim to know exactly what that will look like, but I can imagine it might involve feeling, in full awareness, the sorrow and pain we've caused others in our lifetime. Not as vengeance—but as transformation. Until we fully understand and accept the truth of our wrongs and willingly repent. This process, I believe, is what leads to the day when every knee will bow and every tongue will swear allegiance.

God disciplines us for our good, that we may share in His holiness. No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it.
(Hebrews 12:10-11)

The teachings of the Lord are given so that we might repent now—freely, joyfully, and with open hearts—rather than learning the hard way through painful consequences. Repentance offered today is a gift; delaying it may only mean unnecessary suffering on the path to the same eventual restoration.
Repentance is not merely spoken words or crying eyes—it’s a realignment of our will, our values, and our moral behavior with the heart and character of God.

Think of it like this: a loving parent warns their child about the consequences of reckless choices. The wise child listens—and is spared the pain that follows rebellion. But sometimes, despite all the warnings, the child chooses their own path. When the consequences arrive—like a visit from the authorities or imprisonment—they become the teacher. Suffering opens the door to understanding. And from there, repentance flows.
Christ invites us to skip the needless pain. To follow Him now. To embrace His wisdom and walk the path of repentance—not as punishment, but as the way to true freedom, healing, and joy.
A Different Gospel?

If today’s gospel focuses on escaping endless hellfire torment instead of the early message from the first two centuries about stepping into the life, light, and love of God through Christ, it raises the question: Who altered the biblical message, and for what reason?

The answer is straightforward: if Satan used Scripture in an attempt to tempt and deceive Jesus—if he dared to twist the Bible against Christ Himself—then we can be certain he employs the very same tactic to mislead the Church.

It only makes sense that one of the most effective ways for Satan to distort the gospel is by using the Bible itself. He convinces well-meaning Christians they are being “biblical"—when in reality, they are cherry-picking verses out of context to support their own agendas and theological biases.
And tragically, this kind of selective misuse of Scripture leads people to believe they are preaching the gospel, when in fact, they are driving others away from it.
If this is true—and given how Satan operates, it likely is—then some of the people most in need of salvation are already inside the church.

They need salvation from a distorted image of God—a frightening, wrathful, and condemning figure created by well-meaning Christians who truly believe they are honoring the Bible. They need saving from anxiety and depression, and a path into life.

Sometimes, the greatest deception isn’t outside the church. It’s inside—dressed in religious language, backed by isolated verses, and preached with the best of intentions, but far from the heart of Christ.

wish to leave you with an action point. We must not remain passive and let the I gospel be diminished to merely decoding the right theoretical formula to escape a sadistic, neverending torment in a cosmic inferno. Churches arguing the Gospel is all about escaping a realm of eternal cruel, sadistic, torturous punishment shift focus away from the original message of the Gospel, which we ought to uphold. The message of Christ was about embracing God's love, mercy, and grace and paying them forward.

Rather than getting bogged down in theological debates over the afterlife, we should focus on embodying and radiating God's love in a world riddled with brokenness and despair. God's love is not a formula for escaping torture; it's a call to action, inviting us to participate in healing and restoration. The Gospel, at its core, is about transformation—of hearts, lives, and communities—through the love and grace of God, as revealed in our Messiah Yeshua (Hebrew for Jesus, which also means "salvation’).
